summary: Risperidone is an atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic that antagonizes dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. It is used for schizophrenia, acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder, and irritability associated with autistic disorder. It carries a boxed warning for increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis.
indications: Treatment of schizophrenia (adults and adolescents 13-17 years)
Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder, as monotherapy or adjunct to lithium or valproate (adults; children/adolescents 10-17 years for monotherapy)
Irritability associated with autistic disorder, including aggression, self-injury, temper tantrums, and rapidly changing moods (children/adolescents 5-17 years)

dosage.d: Initial 2 mg/day; target 4-8 mg/day; range 4-16 mg/day
dosage.t: Increase at intervals of >=24 h in increments of 1-2 mg/day; doses >6 mg/day (twice-daily) not more effective and more adverse effects
dosage.n: Once or twice daily; max studied 16 mg/day

dosage.d: Initial 0.5 mg once daily; target 3 mg/day; range 1-6 mg/day
dosage.t: Adjust at intervals of >=24 h by 0.5-1 mg/day; no added benefit above 3 mg/day
dosage.n: Single morning or evening dose; doses >6 mg/day not studied

dosage.t: Adjust at intervals of >=24 h by 1 mg/day

dosage.d: Initial 0.5 mg once daily; target 1-2.5 mg/day; range 1-6 mg/day
dosage.t: Adjust at intervals of >=24 h by 0.5-1 mg/day; no added benefit above 2.5 mg/day

dosage.d: Initial 0.25 mg/day; target 0.5 mg/day; range 0.5-3 mg/day
dosage.t: After >=4 days may increase to 0.5 mg/day; further increases at intervals of >=2 weeks by 0.25 mg/day
dosage.n: No dosing data for children <15 kg

dosage.d: Initial 0.5 mg/day; target 1 mg/day; range 0.5-3 mg/day
dosage.t: After >=4 days may increase to 1 mg/day; further increases at intervals of >=2 weeks by 0.5 mg/day
dosage.n: May give once daily or split twice daily

dosage.t: Increase by <=0.5 mg twice daily; for doses above 1.5 mg twice daily, increase at intervals of >=1 week

admin: Administer orally once or twice daily; may be taken with or without meals.
Adolescents on once-daily dosing may take a single dose in the morning or evening.
Patients with persistent somnolence may take half the daily dose twice daily, or a bedtime dose.
When co-administered with enzyme inducers (e.g., carbamazepine), increase the risperidone dose up to double the usual dose; titrate slowly.
When co-administered with fluoxetine or paroxetine, reduce the dose and do not exceed 8 mg/day in adults.
On reinitiation after discontinuation, follow the initial titration schedule.
moa: The mechanism in schizophrenia is not fully established but is thought to involve combined antagonism of dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. The clinical effect reflects the combined activity of risperidone and its major active metabolite, 9-hydroxyrisperidone (paliperidone). Antagonism at other receptors may account for additional effects.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to risperidone or paliperidone, or to any excipient (anaphylaxis and angioedema reported)
relative: Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies (increased sensitivity, risk of NMS-like features)
Cardiovascular disease or conditions predisposing to hypotension
Diabetes or risk factors for hyperglycemia
Conditions predisposing to QT prolongation or with concomitant QT-prolonging drugs
monitor: BOXED WARNING: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics are at increased risk of death; risperidone is NOT approved for dementia-related psychosis
Watch for cerebrovascular events (stroke) in elderly dementia patients
Monitor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and tardive dyskinesia
Monitor fasting glucose, lipids, and weight
Monitor prolactin-related effects (galactorrhea, gynecomastia, menstrual changes)
Monitor orthostatic vital signs and for falls
Monitor CBC in patients with low WBC or history of leukopenia/neutropenia

preg: Neonates exposed during the third trimester are at risk for extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms (agitation, hypertonia, hypotonia, tremor, somnolence, respiratory distress, feeding disorder); monitor and manage accordingly. Available epidemiologic data have not established a clear drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. Untreated schizophrenia/bipolar I disorder also poses maternal and fetal risks. A pregnancy exposure registry for atypical antipsychotics exists (National Pregnancy Registry, 1-866-961-2388).
lact: Risperidone and 9-hydroxyrisperidone are present in human milk (relative infant dose ~2.3% to 4.7% of weight-adjusted maternal dose). Sedation, failure to thrive, jitteriness, and extrapyramidal symptoms have been reported in breastfed infants. Weigh developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against clinical need and potential effects; monitor the infant for sedation, failure to thrive, jitteriness, and EPS.
renal: In moderate-to-severe renal impairment (ClCr 15-59 mL/min) clearance of the active moiety decreased by ~60%. Reduce the dose: initial 0.5 mg twice daily, with increases of <=0.5 mg twice daily; for doses above 1.5 mg twice daily, titrate at intervals of >=1 week.
hepatic: In liver disease the free fraction of risperidone is increased by ~35%. Reduce the dose: initial 0.5 mg twice daily, with increases of <=0.5 mg twice daily; for doses above 1.5 mg twice daily, titrate at intervals of >=1 week.

major: CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine): increase risperidone levels - reduce dose, do not exceed 8 mg/day in adults
Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin, phenobarbital): decrease risperidone levels - may need up to double the dose; titrate slowly
Levodopa and dopamine agonists: risperidone may antagonize their effects
moderate: Other centrally acting drugs: additive CNS effects
Antihypertensives and other hypotensive agents: enhanced hypotension
Methylphenidate: increased risk of extrapyramidal symptoms with dose changes
Drugs that prolong the QT interval
minor: Ranitidine, cimetidine, erythromycin, amitriptyline: no dose adjustment needed
Lithium, valproate, digoxin: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic effect from risperidone
interactions.food: Food does not affect the rate or extent of absorption; may be given with or without meals.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; additive CNS depression with this centrally acting drug.
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate serum prolactin; can prolong the QT interval and cause ECG changes.

common: Nausea, vomiting, constipation, dyspepsia, abdominal discomfort
Nasal congestion, upper respiratory infection, nasopharyngitis
serious: BOXED WARNING: Increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotic drugs
Cerebrovascular events including stroke in elderly dementia patients
Metabolic changes: hyperglycemia/diabetes, dyslipidemia, weight gain
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis and angioedema
emergency: Increased risk of death in elderly dementia patients (boxed warning) - reassess therapy
Stroke/TIA signs in elderly dementia patients - seek emergency care
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (high fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Extrapyramidal symptoms and signs of tardive dyskinesia
Orthostatic blood pressure and pulse, fall risk
CBC in patients with low WBC or history of neutropenia
Mental status and, in elderly dementia patients, mortality/stroke risk
counsel: May be taken with or without food.
Avoid alcohol and use caution with other sedating medications.
Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how the drug affects you (may cause drowsiness or dizziness).
Rise slowly from sitting or lying to reduce dizziness from low blood pressure.
Report fever with muscle rigidity, uncontrolled movements, or prolonged painful erection immediately.
Avoid overheating and dehydration; the drug can impair temperature regulation.
Report missed periods, breast enlargement, or breast discharge.
Do not stop abruptly without consulting your prescriber.
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially carbamazepine, fluoxetine, or paroxetine.
pearls: BOXED WARNING: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death; risperidone is not approved for dementia-related psychosis.
Clinical effect reflects the combined activity of risperidone plus its active metabolite 9-hydroxyrisperidone (paliperidone).
Metabolized mainly by CYP2D6; poor metabolizers and CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine) increase exposure - cap adult dose at 8 mg/day.
Strong enzyme inducers (carbamazepine) lower levels - may require doubling the dose; adjust again when the inducer is stopped.
More likely than many antipsychotics to raise prolactin and to cause dose-dependent extrapyramidal symptoms.
Doses above 6 mg/day for schizophrenia are generally not more effective and increase EPS.
Patients with Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia can have heightened sensitivity.
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Reported signs reflect exaggerated pharmacologic effects: drowsiness/sedation, tachycardia, hypotension, and extrapyramidal symptoms; QT prolongation, widened QRS, electrolyte disturbances, and seizures have occurred, and torsade de pointes was reported with combined risperidone/paroxetine overdose. There is no specific antidote. Provide supportive care - ensure airway, oxygenation, and ventilation; monitor cardiac rhythm and vital signs; treat symptomatically. Consider multi-drug ingestion. Contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222).
